faqs.answer: Technical SEO is built into well-developed custom websites by default — not added as a plugin or afterthought. Specifically: (1) SSR (server-side rendering with Next.js) ensures every page is fully rendered HTML when Google crawls it — no JavaScript execution delay. (2) JSON-LD structured data on every relevant page type (FAQPage, Article, Product, Organization, BreadcrumbList). (3) Precise canonical tag control. Template platforms require plugins for most of these, creating fragility; custom code implements them correctly from the start.

faqs.question: What makes a website 'custom' vs. template-based?
faqs.answer: A custom website is built from source code, designed from your brand identity, without any commercial theme or template as a starting point. A template-based website customizes an existing theme or template purchased from a marketplace (ThemeForest, Envato) or built into a platform (Squarespace, Wix). The distinction matters because: (1) Design uniqueness — a template is used by thousands of other businesses; a custom design is yours alone. (2) Performance — templates include features you don't use, creating unnecessary code weight; custom code includes only what you need. (3) Flexibility — templates can't be modified beyond their built-in customization options; custom code can be changed in any way. (4) SEO — templates may generate poor HTML structure, duplicate content, or render-blocking code that custom development avoids.

faqs.question: Does Core Web Vitals score directly impact Google search rankings for custom websites?
faqs.answer: Yes — Google confirmed Core Web Vitals as ranking signals in the Page Experience update. The three metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) — measures loading performance; target < 2.5 seconds. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — measures visual stability; target < 0.1. INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — measures responsiveness; target < 200ms (replaced FID in March 2024). Custom websites built with Next.js and proper image optimisation consistently achieve 90+ Lighthouse scores because: (1) next/image automatically serves WebP/AVIF, sets correct dimensions (preventing CLS), and lazy-loads below-the-fold images. (2) SSR/SSG generates fully-rendered HTML — no JavaScript execution before content appears (improving LCP). (3) Code splitting delivers only the code needed for each page (reducing JavaScript parse time). Template-based sites (Squarespace, Wix) frequently score 40–70 on mobile Lighthouse due to unoptimised themes and third-party scripts. For competitive search niches, the Core Web Vitals gap between custom and template sites is a meaningful ranking advantage.

faqs.question: What is the difference between custom website development and web design?
faqs.answer: Web design: the visual and UX discipline — creating the look, feel, layout, typography, colour system, and user interface of a website. Output: Figma mockups, design system documentation. Web development: the engineering discipline — writing the code that implements the design in a browser. Output: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, backend code, deployment configuration. Custom website development combines both: starting from brand identity (no templates), designing in Figma, then engineering the design in code with technical SEO, performance optimisation, CMS integration, and deployment. A web designer who cannot code will hand off Figma files to a separate developer — potentially causing design-to-code inconsistencies. A developer who cannot design will produce technically correct but visually mediocre results. Ramesh handles both: Figma design system creation and full-stack Next.js implementation — ensuring the live website precisely matches the approved design, with no design-to-development translation loss.

faqs.question: How does a custom website developer handle website security?
faqs.answer: Custom website security best practices: (1) HTTPS everywhere — TLS/SSL certificate on all environments (automatic with Vercel/Netlify; configured manually on custom servers). (2) Content Security Policy (CSP) headers — prevents cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks by whitelisting approved script sources. (3) API key security — all third-party API keys stored in environment variables, never in frontend code or Git history. (4) Input validation — all form inputs validated and sanitised on both client and server side. (5) Authentication security — if user accounts are included: JWT tokens with short expiry, secure HTTP-only cookies, CSRF protection, rate limiting on auth endpoints. (6) Dependency security — regular npm audit / dependabot alerts to patch known vulnerabilities. (7) SQL injection prevention — parameterised queries only, never string concatenation in SQL. (8) OWASP Top 10 coverage — the standard checklist of web application security risks, reviewed for every project. Ramesh includes an OWASP ZAP security scan report as a standard deliverable for projects with authentication or payment features.
